---
title: "R → Python"
---

This bridge uses base R vocabulary and the same Python table operations taught in the course. It does not require installing R. The Python code executes in the course build; R expressions here are reading comparisons and have not been run as part of that check. Match samples, keys and model conventions before comparing output.


Tables can be scrolled sideways on a narrow screen.

## Translate intentions

::: {.table-responsive}

| Intention | Familiar R expression | Python approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read CSV | `read.csv(...)` | `pd.read_csv(...)` |
| See column names | `names(d)` | `d.columns` |
| First observations | `head(d)` | `d.head()` |
| Select a year | `subset(d, year == 2007)` | `d.loc[d["year"] == 2007].copy()` |
| Create a transformed variable | `log(d$gdp_pc)` | `np.log(d["gdp_pc"])` |
| Group means | `aggregate(life_exp ~ region, d, mean)` | `groupby("region")["life_exp"].mean()` |
| Join tables | `merge(d, lookup, by="country", all.x=TRUE)` | Explicit left merge with key validation |
| Fit a linear model | `lm(life_exp ~ log_gdp_pc, data=d)` | `smf.ols(..., data=d).fit(...)` |
| Obtain coefficients | `coef(model)` | `model.params` |

:::


These are bridges for the stated complete examples, not universal replacements. R's [subset documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/subset.html) describes evaluation and missingness rules. Its [lm documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/lm.html) describes formula, missing-action and fitting defaults. Ordinary lm uncertainty is not automatically HC1; use an explicitly appropriate covariance method before comparing robust intervals.

## A complete Python sequence

Load the historical country data and inspect its schema. pandas usually uses brackets for named fields rather than R's dollar-field notation.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
d = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder.csv")
print(d.columns.tolist())
print(d.head(2))
```

A DataFrame has both named columns and a row index. The index may be labels rather than observation numbers. For the first row by position use `.iloc[0]`; Python positions begin at zero.

Create an explicit 2007 copy and log the positive income field. Count the retained sample rather than relying on the formula to silently remove observations.

```{python}
selected = d.loc[d["year"] == 2007, ["country", "region", "life_exp", "gdp_pc"]].dropna().copy()
assert selected["gdp_pc"].gt(0).all()
selected["log_gdp_pc"] = np.log(selected["gdp_pc"])
summary = selected.groupby("region")["life_exp"].agg(["count", "mean"])
print(summary.round(2))
```

All 142 countries remain. Each regional mean uses the number in its own count column. R formula aggregation and pandas grouping can treat missing fields and grouping values differently in other data; define the intended denominator explicitly rather than assuming these commands always select identical rows.

Join a known unique lookup with a stated left-join contract. Do not rely on output row order as the meaning of an observation.

```{python}
lookup = d[["country", "region"]].drop_duplicates()
joined = selected.drop(columns="region").merge(lookup, on="country", how="left", validate="one_to_one", indicator=True)
print(joined["_merge"].value_counts())
```

The original selected table has one country row, and so does the lookup. `one_to_one` would be inappropriate for a repeated country panel; that join would use `many_to_one`. Check keys and matches after each sample restriction.

Fit simple and region-adjusted OLS, choosing HC1 t-based approximate inference explicitly.

```{python}
simple = smf.ols("life_exp ~ log_gdp_pc", selected, missing="raise").fit(cov_type="HC1", use_t=True)
adjusted = smf.ols("life_exp ~ log_gdp_pc + C(region)", selected, missing="raise").fit(cov_type="HC1", use_t=True)
print(pd.DataFrame({"simple": simple.params, "region_adjusted": adjusted.params}).round(3))
```

Missing table entries here mean a term was absent from that model; they are not estimated zero coefficients. Formula `C(region)` declares category indicators for statsmodels. In R, ensure the corresponding field has the intended factor treatment. Reference categories and contrast coding can change the displayed coefficients while preserving fitted values.

## Similar-looking operations that need care

- Assignment uses `=` in Python. A comparison uses `==`. Parenthesize combined pandas masks and use `&` or `|`, with one condition per side.
- `.loc` aligns by labels; `.iloc` selects positions. A Series combined with another Series can align on its index, so separately sorting only one input may change a calculation.
- R's NA and pandas' missing values are not ordinary zero values. pandas nullable dtypes and floating NaN also have distinct behaviours; use explicit missingness checks and the codebook.
- A Python function argument such as `how="left"` has a specific default if omitted. Do not assume a similarly named R and Python function share sorting, joining or missing-action defaults.
- A package's covariance or fixed-effects result object has its own field names and conventions. See [regression tables](../lessons/04-regression/06-regression-tables.ipynb) for extraction without retyping results.

The 2007 simple coefficient is about 7.203 years per natural-log unit. Neither porting a formula nor matching its coefficient establishes a causal effect of income. The [sample](../lessons/04-regression/02-correlation-ols.ipynb), units and assumptions remain part of the analysis.

```{python}
#| include: false
assert len(selected) == len(joined) == 142
assert joined["_merge"].eq("both").all()
assert abs(simple.params["log_gdp_pc"] - 7.202801571) < 1e-6
assert abs(adjusted.params["log_gdp_pc"] - 4.630775270) < 1e-6
```
